title: Why Mosquitoes Bite You More Than Your Friends (Science Finally Knows)
description: Animal Secrets #23. Why do mosquitoes bite some people and ignore others? This week a Florida International University team tested 119 volunteers against three dangerous mosquito species and found something nobody expected: not one person attracted all three. We count down the five things that make you a target, from your breath to your skin's own bacteria. Part of the Wild Sketchbook.

scenes.say: You and your friend sit outside. You get ten bites. They get zero. It's not bad luck.

scenes.label: 119 people tested
scenes.say: This week, scientists tested 119 people against three of the most dangerous mosquitoes on Earth. And the answer surprised even them.
So today, five reasons a mosquito picks you. Each one is weirder than the last.

scenes.label: Wait for #1
scenes.say: And stick around for number one. It means the mosquito biting you tonight might ignore you tomorrow. Because it's a different mosquito.

scenes.label: About 10 a year
scenes.say: Okay, first, why should you care? Sharks kill about ten people a year.

scenes.label: 700,000+ a year
scenes.say: Diseases spread by mosquitoes kill more than 700,000. Every single year. That's why scientists call it the deadliest animal alive.

scenes.label: 610,000 in 2024
scenes.say: Malaria alone killed an estimated 610,000 people in 2024. Most of them were little kids in Africa.

scenes.label: 282 million cases
scenes.say: And that same year there were about 282 million malaria cases. All starting with one tiny bite.
So figuring out who mosquitoes choose isn't a silly question. It could save lives. Let's go.

scenes.label: Your breath
scenes.say: Number five: your breath. Every time you breathe out, you send a signal into the air.
Here's the thing. Only the females bite you. They need blood to make their eggs.

scenes.label: Males drink nectar
scenes.say: The males? They just drink nectar and fruit juice. Totally harmless. So every bite you ever got came from a mom-to-be.

scenes.label: 2 to 4 weeks
scenes.say: An adult mosquito only lives about two to four weeks. So she has very little time to find you.

scenes.label: Up to 15 m
scenes.say: And she finds you with her feathery antennae. They pick up the carbon dioxide in your breath from 10, even 15 meters away.
From that far, she can also smell your skin and even see a fuzzy blob of your body. Creepy, right?
That's across a whole backyard. Your breath is basically a giant arrow saying: dinner is over here.
But wait. Your friend breathes too. So breath can't be the whole story. Something else is going on.

scenes.label: Iceland, 2025
scenes.say: Quick side story. Until last year, Iceland had no mosquitoes at all. Then, in October 2025, a man was setting wine-soaked ropes to catch moths.

scenes.label: 3 mosquitoes
scenes.say: On the ropes he found three mosquitoes. Two females and one male. Iceland's first ever in the wild.

scenes.label: Record heat
scenes.say: It came after Iceland's record-breaking hot spring. And this species is one of the few that can survive the winter.
Now only one place on Earth has no recorded mosquitoes. Antarctica. Think about that next time you complain about your backyard.

scenes.label: Your body heat
scenes.say: Number four: your body heat. And this one sounds like science fiction.

scenes.label: Up to 70 cm
scenes.say: In 2024, scientists showed that mosquitoes can sense the infrared heat glowing off your body. From up to 70 centimeters away.
That's like a tiny heat camera on the tip of each antenna. You glow, and she sees it.
Scientists traced it to a heat-sensing protein called TRPA1, sitting right at the very tip of the antenna.

scenes.label: Under 10 cm
scenes.say: Before that, scientists thought mosquitoes only felt warm air rising off skin. That only works closer than 10 centimeters.
But here's the twist. The heat trick only switched on when the mosquito also smelled breath and human odor. Heat alone? She didn't care.
So she's stacking clues. Breath from far away. Then smell. Then heat. Then she lands and tastes your skin with her legs.

scenes.label: Tastes with legs
scenes.say: Yep, her legs have taste sensors. She's checking the menu before she orders. Gross, right?

scenes.label: Last night
scenes.say: Number three: what you did last night. Scientists actually set up a mosquito lab at a giant music festival.

scenes.label: 465 people
scenes.say: At the 2023 Lowlands festival in the Netherlands, 465 people put their arms against a box full of mosquitoes. On purpose.
A camera counted how many mosquitoes tried to land on each arm. Then people answered questions about their weekend.

scenes.label: Beer = more bites
scenes.say: People who'd had a beer drew more mosquitoes than people who hadn't. And it wasn't how drunk they were. The researchers think it was how they smelled.

scenes.label: 48% less
scenes.say: Now the good news. People who had showered and put on sunscreen were 48 percent less attractive. Soap actually helps.

scenes.label: Blood type?
scenes.say: And what about blood type? You've heard type O gets bitten more, right? In this study, they found no link with blood type at all.
Careful though. That study was a preprint, so other scientists are still checking it. And almost everyone still got a few landings.
So showering helps. But some people still get eaten alive no matter what. Why? That's number two.

scenes.label: Your skin smell
scenes.say: Number two: the smell of your skin. And to test it, scientists in New York used nylon stockings.

scenes.label: 64 volunteers
scenes.say: 64 volunteers wore nylon stockings on their forearms. The nylon trapped their skin smell.
Then the team gave mosquitoes a choice between two stockings. Again and again. Like a dating show, but for mosquitoes.
They even tested mosquitoes with parts of their smell system switched off. Those mosquitoes were way less interested in people, but could still pick out the magnets.

scenes.label: Subject 33
scenes.say: One person, called subject 33, blew everyone away. Their stocking was four times more attractive than the next best person.

scenes.label: 100x more
scenes.say: And over 100 times more attractive than the two least attractive people. Same mosquitoes, same room. Just a different smell.

scenes.label: Carboxylic acids
scenes.say: So what was different? The mosquito magnets made way more carboxylic acids on their skin. Those are fatty acids, linked to your skin's natural oil.

scenes.label: 2 more groups
scenes.say: And they checked it again with two separate groups of volunteers. Same pattern both times.
And here's the scary part. It didn't change. People stayed in the study for years.

scenes.label: Magnet for years
scenes.say: As one scientist put it, if they were a mosquito magnet, they remained a mosquito magnet.
Their lives changed. The seasons changed. The magnets stayed magnets. It's a bit like a smell fingerprint.
So that's it, right? Some people smell great to mosquitoes, and that's that. Well, that's what everyone thought. Until this week.

scenes.label: Which mosquito?
scenes.say: Number one: it depends on which mosquito. And this study just came out.

scenes.label: 3 species
scenes.say: A team at Florida International University tested 119 people against three mosquito species. Each one spreads diseases like dengue, Zika or West Nile.
Here's why that matters. It was the first study to directly compare several mosquito species on the exact same people.

scenes.label: Not one person
scenes.say: And here's the result. Not a single person attracted all three species. Not one out of 119.
Each mosquito had its own favorite people. Your mosquito magnet friend? Maybe only for one kind.

scenes.label: No perfume
scenes.say: The yellow fever mosquito liked people who weren't wearing added fragrance. And it had a slight preference for men.

scenes.label: Plant-like smell
scenes.say: The Asian tiger mosquito went for people whose skin gave off more ketones and plant-like chemicals.

scenes.label: Night biter
scenes.say: And the southern house mosquito, the one that bites at night? It cared most about the bacteria living on your skin.

scenes.label: Skin bacteria
scenes.say: Some bacteria made people more attractive. Other bacteria pushed the mosquitoes away. Your skin's tiny roommates decide if you get bitten.

scenes.label: 1,000+ chemicals
scenes.say: Your skin releases more than 1,000 different smelly chemicals. And each mosquito reads a different part of that mix.
Even the scientists didn't see it coming. The lead researcher said they didn't expect the species to prefer different people.
Her team leader put it like this: our skin bacteria define our smell signature, and each species found its own way to decode it.

scenes.label: Custom repellent?
scenes.say: So why does this matter? Because one day, repellents could be made for the exact mosquito in your area. Not one spray for all.
And with hundreds of thousands of lives on the line every year, that's a big deal.
So let's recap. Your breath calls her. Your heat guides her. Your weekend matters. Your skin oil matters.
And the bacteria on your skin might make you a magnet for one mosquito, and invisible to another.
So your friend with zero bites? Maybe tonight's mosquito just isn't their type. Tomorrow, a different one shows up.

scenes.label: Tell me below
scenes.say: Now I want to know. Are you the mosquito magnet in your group, or the lucky one? Tell me in the comments.

short.title: Not One of 119 People Attracted All 3 Mosquitoes
short.description: A new Florida International University study tested 119 volunteers against three dangerous mosquito species. Not one person attracted all three — each species picked its own favorites, partly by reading the bacteria on our skin. The full countdown of why mosquitoes bite you is on the channel. Part of the Wild Sketchbook.

scenes.say: Not one of 119 people actually attracted all three mosquitoes. Scientists just found out why.

scenes.label: No perfume
scenes.say: The yellow fever mosquito liked people with no added perfume, and slightly preferred men.

scenes.label: Plant-like smell
scenes.say: The Asian tiger mosquito picked people whose skin smelled more like plants.

scenes.label: Skin bacteria
scenes.say: And the night-biting house mosquito? It chose people by the bacteria living on their skin.

scenes.label: 1,000+ chemicals
scenes.say: Your skin gives off more than 1,000 chemicals, and each mosquito reads a different part of the mix. So that friend who never gets bitten? Wrong mosquito.
This could lead to repellents made for one exact mosquito. Are you a magnet? Comment below.
